scoreNote: Strong (5): grants that demanding circumstances produce leaders while arguing that demands can only develop a capacity already present and willingly offered; concrete examples and a clear synthesis.

sentences.text: We often wonder whether great leaders are born or made, and the statement offers a confident answer: that they are made, created by the demands placed upon them.
On this view, ordinary people become leaders because circumstances call forth abilities they would otherwise never have shown.

Demanding circumstances do play a powerful role in producing leaders, but the statement claims too much, because the demands of a situation reveal and develop leadership only in those who already possess the capacity to meet them.
It is true that circumstances summon leadership that might otherwise have lain dormant.
Lincoln might have remained a competent country lawyer had the Civil War not demanded a statesman, and Churchill's defiance found its purpose only when his nation faced destruction.
A crisis raises the stakes and the expectations, forcing people to grow into responsibilities they never sought and revealing reserves of courage and judgment they did not know they had.
Ordinary times rarely produce extraordinary leaders, precisely because they make no extraordinary demands.
Many a quiet figure has become decisive in an emergency, then faded again once the emergency had passed.
Peace and plenty rarely produce a Lincoln, because they ask so little of anyone.
So the statement captures something real: without demands, much potential leadership is never called into being.

sections.role: Body — But demands cannot create capacity from nothing

sentences.text: However, demands cannot create what is not there to be developed.
The same crisis that elevates one person paralyzes or destroys another, which would be impossible if circumstances simply manufactured leaders.
Two officers face the same battle: one rises to command while the other panics, and the difference lies not in the demand but in the people who met it.
Demands test and develop leadership, but the qualities they draw on — courage, judgment, the ability to inspire — must already exist in some form to be drawn upon.
A situation can call for a leader without producing one, as many a leaderless crisis painfully shows.
History is full of moments that cried out for greatness and received only the ordinary people who happened to be in charge.
The throne does not make the king; it merely shows the world whether he can wear it.
The demand sets the stage, but the person must be able to fill it.

sections.role: Body — Leaders are made by demand, ability, and choice

sentences.text: Moreover, the statement leaves out the leader's own choices, which neither circumstance nor character fully explains.
Faced with the same demands and equipped with the same gifts, one person steps forward and another holds back, and that decision is the leader's own.
Leadership is forged where demanding circumstances, latent ability, and a deliberate willingness to answer the call all meet.
To say leaders are merely created by demands is to forget the courage it takes to respond to them.
In conclusion, the demands placed on people do much to create leaders, but not by themselves.
Circumstances summon and shape leadership, yet they can only develop a capacity that already exists and is willingly offered, so leaders are made by demand, ability, and choice together.
The occasion may make the leader possible, but it is the person who decides to become one.
